answer.question: What matters when placing a putting green in Castle Pines?
answer.answer: Look at the available grade, tree roots, access and intended putting lines together. Decide what you want to practice and what landscape will remain. Bring the requirements for your particular community; the City of Castle Pines and the Village at Castle Pines are separate jurisdictions.

blocks.h2: Fit the green to the yard and the shots.
paras: Choose the direction and length of your putts, then discuss cups, contours and fringe. On a wooded or sloping property, a smaller accessible green may be more useful than one that requires major changes to the setting.
Plan for needles and leaves to be cleared, and identify trees or roots that could constrain preparation. Shade can affect how the area is used, but it does not remove the need for regular care.

blocks.h2: Use the requirements for the right property.
paras: The City of Castle Pines and the Village at Castle Pines have different districts and property requirements. Give the exact address and association name when checking the proposed landscape change. Obtain written conditions before finalizing the layout.

Discuss grading, drainage and work near the home as well as the turf surface. If the property has wildfire-related landscape guidance, check material placement with the responsible local team rather than assuming synthetic turf satisfies it.

blocks.h2: A Weiskopf course in the city, two Nicklaus courses next door.
paras: The Ridge at Castle Pines North, a Tom Weiskopf design in the city, is a public course known for large, rolling greens, with views to Pikes Peak and downtown Denver (The Ridge at Castle Pines North). Just south, in the gated Village at Castle Pines, sit Castle Pines Golf Club, Jack Nicklaus's 1981 design and home of The International from 1986 to 2006, and the Country Club at Castle Pines, the community's second Nicklaus course (Wikipedia).

A backyard green here gets built around the way you putt, with the break and the number of cups you choose. On a sloped, treed lot it goes where the grade and the light allow, and the rest of the yard can stay natural.

The city and the Village are separate places. Castle Pines became a city in 2008 and took its current name in 2010, while the Village is an unincorporated community to the south with its own districts and covenants (Wikipedia).

blocks.h2: Two districts, two very different water bills.
paras: In the city, Castle Pines North Metropolitan District allows outdoor watering three days a week through September in 2026, with days assigned by address, and bans runoff, overspray and leaks (CPNMD). Its sod replacement rebate pays up to $3.00 a square foot on homes but requires roughly half the design to be ColoradoScape plant material, so a turf-only conversion looks unlikely to qualify. If you pair turf with planted beds, ask the district in writing whether the planted part can earn it (CPNMD).

In the Village, the water comes entirely from non-renewable groundwater in the Denver Basin aquifers, pumped from 13 wells (Castle Pines Village Metropolitan District). There are no mandatory watering days as of September 2026; instead each lot gets a water budget based on its turf, beds and native grass, with turf allotted 18 gallons a square foot a season and native grass none.

Go over budget and the price climbs from $6.75 per 1,000 gallons to $31.50 above 140%, and the district urges residents to reduce the turf on their property (Castle Pines Village Metropolitan District). How artificial turf counts in a lot's budget isn't published, so ask the district before you plan around it.

blocks.h2: The backyard is protected. The details go through your HOA.
paras: HOA coverage is effectively universal in the city's Castle Pines North neighborhoods and total in the Village. For a detached home, state law bars guidelines that prohibit nonvegetative turf out back, and the association has to offer at least three preapproved front-yard garden plans (SB23-178); the rule skips attached homes and condominiums.

The association's architectural approval still governs materials, color, edging and drainage, and the front yard stays its call. In the Village, landscape changes need the design committee's written approval, and it meets at 8 a.m. on the third Wednesday of each month, so that date sets your start (The Village at Castle Pines). Its public page doesn't mention artificial turf, so confirm with the committee first.
Common areas are a separate case in both places: state law keeps new decorative turf off HOA common grounds, while community playing fields are an exempt category (SB24-005).

faq.q: Who installs artificial turf in Castle Pines, CO?
faq.a: We install backyard putting greens, artificial turf and pet turf in Castle Pines, CO. The Ridge at Castle Pines North is in the city, with Castle Pines Golf Club and a second Nicklaus course in the Village just south. In the city, CPNMD's sod replacement rebate requires roughly half the design in plants, so turf alone is unlikely to earn it. Call 303-349-2368 for a free estimate.

faq.q: When can I water in the city of Castle Pines?
faq.a: Three days a week through September in 2026, on days set by your address; the district posts the day pairs as a graphic (CPNMD). Drip can run any time, and trees, shrubs and gardens can be hand-watered with a shut-off nozzle.

faq.q: Is Castle Pines Golf Club in the city of Castle Pines?
faq.a: No. It's in the Village at Castle Pines, the unincorporated community to the south, and the city's own course is The Ridge at Castle Pines North (Wikipedia).

faq.q: Do new sod and plants get extra water in Castle Pines?
faq.a: In the city, new sod or plants get a 21-day exemption, though not in July or August, and new installations should avoid watering between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. (CPNMD). Turf needs no establishment period at all.
